items.title: Structured Authority Injection: Persistent Human Control for LLM Agents via Typed MCP Overrides
items.summary: 预印本（7 月 27 日提交）提出 Structured Authority Injection（SAI）：把人类操作者的纠正指令改为经类型化、schema 校验的 MCP 工具调用下发，并在每次提示前附加一个带优先级的“权威上下文”。协议定义 Constraint、Priority、Strategy 三类覆盖及其持久化语义和显式优先级，通过规划过程无法访问的定向通道传递。作者称在 9 个模型、8 个针对 agent 失败模式的场景中，减少了指令歧义、缓解多轮规划中的“权威衰减”，最强模型的提示开销最多降低 38%（随模型与场景差异较大）；方法无需微调或访问权重，适用于支持 MCP 工具调用的指令微调模型。
items.why_it_matters: 你关注工具调用与本地部署：该方案不依赖模型权重，把人工干预做成带 schema 的 MCP 调用，可作为后端 agent 平台“人工审批 / 优先级覆盖”接口的设计参考；但收益在不同模型间差别很大，不宜把 38% 当作通用指标。

items.title: Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution
items.summary: 预印本（10 月 15 日提交）提出 Harness-Delta Attribution（HDA），把 agent harness（提示词、技能、工具与编排代码）自动演化带来的提升拆分为三部分：基准特定的过拟合、测试时算力增加、以及剩余可泛化部分。作者在 11 个执行模型、3 个 harness 演化框架，覆盖数学、编程、创意与 agent 任务：21 个出现显著搜索集提升的设定中，过拟合与测试时扩展平均分别解释 54% 和 14%，其中 14 个设定二者合计超过 50%；搜索集增益常无法迁移到留出任务，仅靠验证集信号不足以防止过拟合。
items.why_it_matters: 若你在迭代 prompt 与工具链，这篇提示要单独核算“多跑几轮 / 多给 token”带来的收益，否则容易在自建评测集上过拟合，把不可迁移的涨点当作真实改进。

{"id": "f34ad45741b405ff9e69", "title": "Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution", "url": "https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22466", "source_id": "arxiv", "source": "arXiv cs.AI / cs.LG", "published_at": "2026-10-19T04:00:00+00:00", "text": "Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.22466 (cs) [Submitted on 15 Oct 2026] Title: Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution Authors: Wenxuan Ding , Qin Lu , Changlong Yu , Sha Li , Shuowei Jin , Xin Liu , Zhenyu Shi , Greg Durrett View a PDF of the paper titled Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution, by Wenxuan Ding and 7 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Harness evolution automatically optimizes the prompts, skills, tools, and orchestration code around a fixed-weight model, offering a way to improve agentic systems without updating model weights. The agent harness is iteratively optimized to achieve higher performance on the search set. But how much of this gain reflects benchmark-specific overfitting or additional inference-time compute, and how much may generalize beyond the search set? In this work, we introduce Harness-Delta Attribution (HDA), an evaluation protocol that dissects an evolution gain into artifact-driven overfitting, gains explained by test-time scaling, and the remainder, which gives an upper bound on residual generalizable improvement. We apply HDA to 11 executor models and three harness-evolution frameworks across math, coding, creativity, and agentic tasks. In 21 of these settings that show statistically significant search-set gains, we find that a large share of the improvement is explained by overfitting or test-time scaling. Specifically, among these 21 settings, overfitting and test-time scaling account for 54% and 14% of the gain on average; their combined share exceeds 50% in 14 settings. The residual and held-out transfer vary substantially across tasks, models, and frameworks. Importantly, search-set gains often fail to transfer to held-out tasks, and provide limited evidence that they will persist under practical distribution shifts. Moreover, validation-based signals are insufficient to prevent overfitting. These results motivate attribution-aware evaluation in future harness evolution research. selected_evidence.title: Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution
selected_evidence.text: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.22466 (cs) [Submitted on 15 Oct 2026] Title: Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution Authors: Wenxuan Ding , Qin Lu , Changlong Yu , Sha Li , Shuowei Jin , Xin Liu , Zhenyu Shi , Greg Durrett View a PDF of the paper titled Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution, by Wenxuan Ding and 7 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Harness evolution automatically optimizes the prompts, skills, tools, and orchestration code around a fixed-weight model, offering a way to improve agentic systems without updating model weights. The agent harness is iteratively optimized to achieve higher performance on the search set. But how much of this gain reflects benchmark-specific overfitting or additional inference-time compute, and how much may generalize beyond the search set? In this work, we introduce Harness-Delta Attribution (HDA), an evaluation protocol that dissects an evolution gain into artifact-driven overfitting, gains explained by test-time scaling, and the remainder, which gives an upper bound on residual generalizable improvement. We apply HDA to 11 executor models and three harness-evolution frameworks across math, coding, creativity, and agentic tasks. In 21 of these settings that show statistically significant search-set gains, we find that a large share of the improvement is explained by overfitting or test-time scaling. Specifically, among these 21 settings, overfitting and test-time scaling account for 54% and 14% of the gain on average; their combined share exceeds 50% in 14 settings. The residual and held-out transfer vary substantially across tasks, models, and frameworks. Importantly, search-set gains often fail to transfer to held-out tasks, and provide limited evidence that they will persist under practical distribution shifts. Moreover, validation-based signals are insufficient to prevent overfitting. These results motivate attribution-aware evaluation in future harness evolution research. brief.title: AI 研究简报 · 2026-10-19｜聚焦评测方法：基准增益归因、Agent 规划可信度、日常推理基准
brief.overview: 过去 24 小时内，OpenAI、Google、Hugging Face、TechCrunch 四个来源的 RSS 均无窗口内条目（返回为空），可用内容集中在 arXiv cs.AI / cs.LG 的 40 篇新论文。按你的「研究论文 / 模型评测 / 机器学习 + benchmark、evaluation」偏好，本期只挑选 3 篇直接讨论评测效度的预印本（均为 v1，未经同行评审，结论以其自述实验条件为准）：一是把「harness 进化」的涨点拆解为过拟合与测试时算力；二是用形式化语义检验 Agent 的规划宣称；三是用语言学/语用现象构建「日常逻辑推理」基准并对比推理模型与非推理模型。本期无融资类内容。

items.title: Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution
items.summary: 论文提出 Harness-Delta Attribution（HDA）评测协议，用于拆解「harness 进化」（在冻结模型权重下自动优化提示词、技能、工具与编排代码）在搜索集上的增益，将其分解为三部分：产物驱动的过拟合、可由测试时算力扩展解释的部分、以及剩余部分（作为可泛化改进的上界）。作者在 11 个执行模型、3 个 harness 进化框架、覆盖数学/编程/创造性/Agent 任务上运行该协议；在 21 个搜索集增益统计显著的设置中，过拟合平均解释 54%、测试时扩展解释 14%，二者合计在 14 个设置中超过 50%；搜索集增益常无法迁移到留出任务，且仅靠验证集信号不足以阻止过拟合。
items.why_it_matters: 直接针对你关心的 benchmark 与评测效度：它提供可复用的归因式评测流程，可用于审视「不训练权重、只改 harness 就涨点」类结论，避免把过拟合或更多推理算力误读为能力提升；方法本身也可作为你自己设计评测消融的模板。

items.title: Testing the Planning Claims of LLM-Based Agents against Formal Semantics
items.summary: 作者不用端到端成功率或 LLM 评审，而是把任务置于隐藏的 PDDL 形式模型下，逐动作校验可适用性、目标达成与可解性。实验覆盖 5 个领域（含 2 个新领域，随论文发布）、4 个模型、6 种提示策略、3 种 Agent 架构：最佳配置离线解出 78% 的可解任务，在线（需实际观察状态）仅 40%，Agent 多数情况下不检查状态；不可解任务仅在不到 10% 的回合中被识别；更重的提示策略消耗 5–22 倍 token 却无明确收益；规划表现跨模型的差异大于跨提示策略与架构的差异。
items.why_it_matters: 为「Agent 会规划」这类宣称提供了可验证的动作轨迹证据要求，指出离线规划准确率与在线执行之间存在约 38 个百分点的落差——若你在做 Agent 基准或引用规划类指标，这篇提示应区分离线/在线设定并报告 token 成本。

items.title: Are Large Reasoning Models Good Everyday Reasoners? A Comparison with Non-Reasoning Models on Logical Reasoning Tasks
items.summary: 论文基于语言学与语用学推理现象构建「日常逻辑推理」基准，在受控提示条件下比较大型推理模型（LRM，依赖测试时计算）与非推理模型。结果显示：当日常推理偏离教科书形式逻辑规则时，推理模型表现下降；部分非推理模型配合思维链提示可超过同等规模的推理模型；追加指令提示对推理行为的控制力有限。作者据此认为当前推理模型未能可靠覆盖日常推理，并指向后训练目标与评测多样性的局限。
items.why_it_matters: 这是一份新的、与形式逻辑基准互补的评测集，可用于检查推理模型在你关心的场景里是否存在「形式题强、语用题弱」的盲区；对设计后训练数据与多类型推理评测的研究者具直接参考价值。

{"id": "f34ad45741b405ff9e69", "title": "Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution", "url": "https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22466", "source_id": "arxiv", "source": "arXiv cs.AI / cs.LG", "published_at": "2026-10-19T04:00:00+00:00", "text": "Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.22466 (cs) [Submitted on 15 Oct 2026] Title: Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution Authors: Wenxuan Ding , Qin Lu , Changlong Yu , Sha Li , Shuowei Jin , Xin Liu , Zhenyu Shi , Greg Durrett View a PDF of the paper titled Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution, by Wenxuan Ding and 7 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Harness evolution automatically optimizes the prompts, skills, tools, and orchestration code around a fixed-weight model, offering a way to improve agentic systems without updating model weights. The agent harness is iteratively optimized to achieve higher performance on the search set. But how much of this gain reflects benchmark-specific overfitting or additional inference-time compute, and how much may generalize beyond the search set? In this work, we introduce Harness-Delta Attribution (HDA), an evaluation protocol that dissects an evolution gain into artifact-driven overfitting, gains explained by test-time scaling, and the remainder, which gives an upper bound on residual generalizable improvement. We apply HDA to 11 executor models and three harness-evolution frameworks across math, coding, creativity, and agentic tasks. In 21 of these settings that show statistically significant search-set gains, we find that a large share of the improvement is explained by overfitting or test-time scaling. Specifically, among these 21 settings, overfitting and test-time scaling account for 54% and 14% of the gain on average; their combined share exceeds 50% in 14 settings. The residual and held-out transfer vary substantially across tasks, models, and frameworks. Importantly, search-set gains often fail to transfer to held-out tasks, and provide limited evidence that they will persist under practical distribution shifts. Moreover, validation-based signals are insufficient to prevent overfitting. These results motivate attribution-aware evaluation in future harness evolution research. {"id": "8cad1d7071d358947cb2", "title": "Testing the Planning Claims of LLM-Based Agents against Formal Semantics", "url": "https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22469", "source_id": "arxiv", "source": "arXiv cs.AI / cs.LG", "published_at": "2026-10-19T04:00:00+00:00", "text": "Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.22469 (cs) [Submitted on 15 Oct 2026] Title: Testing the Planning Claims of LLM-Based Agents against Formal Semantics Authors: Oriol Miro-Lopez-Feliu , Oscar Miró López-Feliu , Victor Gimenez-Abalos , Javier Vazquez-Salceda , Victor Carballo Araruna , Sergio Alvarez-Napagao View a PDF of the paper titled Testing the Planning Claims of LLM-Based Agents against Formal Semantics, by Oriol Miro-Lopez-Feliu and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly credited with the competences of practical reasoning: planning, monitoring, and correcting their own actions. Their success is attributed to the prompting strategies and agent architectures built around the model, such as chain-of-thought, search-based prompting, self-refinement, reflection, critics and tool-using loops. Yet these claims are usually supported by end-to-end success rates, which show only whether a task was completed, or by LLM judges, which are not verifiers. We test LLM planning against formal semantics. Tasks are posed in natural language, but each is grounded in a hidden PDDL model that decides whether every action is applicable, whether the goal is reached, and whether a plan exists at all. Across five domains (two of them new, all released with the paper), four models, six prompting strategies and three agent architectures, the best configuration solves 78% of the solvable tasks offline but only 40% online, where agents mostly act without inspecting the state. Unsolvable tasks are recognised in under 10% of episodes, and heavier prompting strategies use 5 to 22 times as many tokens as direct prompting with no clear gain. In our experiments, planning performance varied more across models than across prompting strategies or agent architectures. Claims that agents can plan require evidence from validated action traces. A Comparison with Non-Reasoning Models on Logical Reasoning Tasks, by Kentaro Ozeki and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) that leverage test-time computation achieve strong performance on mathematical and scientific benchmarks and are increasingly deployed in real-world applications. A Comparison with Non-Reasoning Models on Logical Reasoning Tasks, by Kentaro Ozeki and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) that leverage test-time computation achieve strong performance on mathematical and scientific benchmarks and are increasingly deployed in real-world applications. However, their ability to perform \textit{everyday logical reasoning}, which often departs from textbook formal logic, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically evaluate how well reasoning models align with everyday reasoning patterns by introducing a benchmark based on linguistic and pragmatic reasoning phenomena. We also compare reasoning models with non-reasoning models under controlled prompting conditions. We find that, in many cases, (1) reasoning models show degraded performance in everyday reasoning when such reasoning deviates from formal logical rules, (2) some non-reasoning models with chain-of-thought prompting outperform comparable reasoning models in everyday reasoning, and (3) prompting with additional instructions provides limited control over reasoning behavior. These findings suggest that current reasoning models do not reliably capture everyday reasoning and point to limitations in post-training, motivating improved training objectives and evaluation across diverse forms of reasoning. selected_evidence.title: Testing the Planning Claims of LLM-Based Agents against Formal Semantics
selected_evidence.text: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.22469 (cs) [Submitted on 15 Oct 2026] Title: Testing the Planning Claims of LLM-Based Agents against Formal Semantics Authors: Oriol Miro-Lopez-Feliu , Oscar Miró López-Feliu , Victor Gimenez-Abalos , Javier Vazquez-Salceda , Victor Carballo Araruna , Sergio Alvarez-Napagao View a PDF of the paper titled Testing the Planning Claims of LLM-Based Agents against Formal Semantics, by Oriol Miro-Lopez-Feliu and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly credited with the competences of practical reasoning: planning, monitoring, and correcting their own actions. Their success is attributed to the prompting strategies and agent architectures built around the model, such as chain-of-thought, search-based prompting, self-refinement, reflection, critics and tool-using loops. Yet these claims are usually supported by end-to-end success rates, which show only whether a task was completed, or by LLM judges, which are not verifiers. We test LLM planning against formal semantics. Tasks are posed in natural language, but each is grounded in a hidden PDDL model that decides whether every action is applicable, whether the goal is reached, and whether a plan exists at all. Across five domains (two of them new, all released with the paper), four models, six prompting strategies and three agent architectures, the best configuration solves 78% of the solvable tasks offline but only 40% online, where agents mostly act without inspecting the state. Unsolvable tasks are recognised in under 10% of episodes, and heavier prompting strategies use 5 to 22 times as many tokens as direct prompting with no clear gain. In our experiments, planning performance varied more across models than across prompting strategies or agent architectures. Claims that agents can plan require evidence from validated action traces. selected_evidence.title: Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution
selected_evidence.text: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.22466 (cs) [Submitted on 15 Oct 2026] Title: Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution Authors: Wenxuan Ding , Qin Lu , Changlong Yu , Sha Li , Shuowei Jin , Xin Liu , Zhenyu Shi , Greg Durrett View a PDF of the paper titled Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution, by Wenxuan Ding and 7 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Harness evolution automatically optimizes the prompts, skills, tools, and orchestration code around a fixed-weight model, offering a way to improve agentic systems without updating model weights. The agent harness is iteratively optimized to achieve higher performance on the search set. But how much of this gain reflects benchmark-specific overfitting or additional inference-time compute, and how much may generalize beyond the search set? In this work, we introduce Harness-Delta Attribution (HDA), an evaluation protocol that dissects an evolution gain into artifact-driven overfitting, gains explained by test-time scaling, and the remainder, which gives an upper bound on residual generalizable improvement. We apply HDA to 11 executor models and three harness-evolution frameworks across math, coding, creativity, and agentic tasks. In 21 of these settings that show statistically significant search-set gains, we find that a large share of the improvement is explained by overfitting or test-time scaling. Specifically, among these 21 settings, overfitting and test-time scaling account for 54% and 14% of the gain on average; their combined share exceeds 50% in 14 settings. The residual and held-out transfer vary substantially across tasks, models, and frameworks. Importantly, search-set gains often fail to transfer to held-out tasks, and provide limited evidence that they will persist under practical distribution shifts. Moreover, validation-based signals are insufficient to prevent overfitting. These results motivate attribution-aware evaluation in future harness evolution research.
